title: VMware
subtitle: Virtual machines, the free Player and ready-made appliances
description: On the show's first anniversary, Steve recaps what virtual machines are and why they matter for security, then tours VMware: Workstation, the bare-metal ESX server, the free VMware Player and its downloadable "appliances," including a ready-to-run Ubuntu browser. He explains snapshots for track-free browsing and why a VM keeps malware in a sandbox.

beats.t: It's Thursday, so it's time for our security czar, Steve Gibson.
And now I'm the birthday czar. This is the official anniversary: Episode 53.
It doesn't seem like a year, and I expect we'll go on for many more. Security isn't going anywhere.
With Vista coming, we'll be busy.
Three weeks ago we started on virtualization. Shall we recap?
I worried people wouldn't care about our walk down memory lane, but lots of you enjoyed the history: emulators, UCSD Pascal and all that.
We remember 4.77 megahertz, and we were happy to have it!
The best definition: a virtual machine is software pretending to be a computer, a computer running within a computer.
The old way was pure emulation. Even BASIC was often compiled into "byte code," a pseudo machine language that the interpreter executed as if it were hardware.

For security, the point is that software in the virtual computer isn't running on the raw hardware unconstrained, so you can put limits around it. That's "sandboxing": a restricted environment where software can do useful things but not harmful ones.
It can be pure software, a hybrid, or in theory pure hardware.
And new Intel processors support it in hardware, so the penalty is much smaller.
I predict we're on the cusp of a big rise in virtual computing. It died out for a couple of decades, then came back as RAM, drives and processors grew enough to absorb the overhead.
VMware was early to take the Intel processor, which wasn't designed for virtualization, and figure out how to trap privileged instructions that normally can't be trapped.
It has 20 or 30 patents on workarounds. Now Intel, and surely AMD, are making the hardware friendlier, so VMware is losing some of that advantage.
Operating systems are also absorbing it. I expect Linux to add more virtualization soon. FreeBSD already has "jails": you can log in as root, but you're a jailed root user who can't get out.
Rumor says Apple might add it to Leopard, due next spring. They didn't mention it at the Worldwide Developers Conference, but said they weren't showing everything.
And at that conference, VMware announced VMware for the Mac. You can sign up for the beta.

beats.title: VMware Fusion
beats.t: The Mac version shipped as VMware Fusion in August 2007. Leopard arrived in October 2007 without built-in virtualization; Apple offered Boot Camp for running Windows natively instead.
We both use Parallels to run Windows on our Intel Macs, and I'm very happy with it.
It's very VMware-like; even the icons look similar. What's special about VMware is that every product in its line can run the same virtual machines.
These programs don't take a partition. They create one large file that looks like a hard drive. So I could copy my Windows file to a Linux box with VMware and run it there?
Yes. I've long used VMware to evaluate personal firewalls. A firewall sinks its roots into your kernel, and after uninstalling you're never sure it's all gone.
And each test starts from an identical system.

In VMware Workstation you press a power button and watch a virtual BIOS count memory and boot. I install Windows and my apps, save it, then stamp out copies like cookies: ten identical machines named ZoneAlarm, Kerio, Norton, McAfee and so on, each with one firewall installed.
A tabbed interface jumps instantly between them. They can network with each other and the host, share files and drag and drop. If I forgot to test something, I just click through all ten.
You need a big hard drive.
And a contemporary machine. You can't run it on your grandmother's computer.
And lots of RAM, since you're running two operating systems at once.

You can pause, suspend or shut down a VM. The result is a master .vmx file, maybe 300 or 400 megabytes, that any VMware product can run. Just don't stamp your licensed copy of Windows all over the place. With open-source software, you can share it freely.
Windows activation travels inside the VM, so moving it to another host doesn't change the "machine."
VMware also has ESX, which installs directly on bare hardware. It started from Linux and is moving to VMware's own code.
No operating system needed at all?

None. Hosting companies can run up to 128 virtual machines on one server, each sandboxed with controlled access to the disk. When a client leaves, delete their VM and stamp out a new one from a template.
How close to full speed is it?
On good hardware, you really can't tell the difference.
Parallels runs snappily on my 2GB MacBook. Adobe Audition with many tracks and voice dictation both work fine.

beats.title: Hypervisors
beats.t: ESX is a "type 1" hypervisor that runs directly on hardware. Workstation, Player and Parallels are "type 2," running on top of a host OS. Today's cloud services run on type 1 hypervisors like ESXi, KVM, Xen and Hyper-V.
Here's where security comes in: VMs are super secure, and they also give you privacy.
VMware can discard all changes when you power off. Every boot starts from the original image.
So it throws out any changes you make.

It keeps them during your session, but not across sessions. Browsers save cookies, cached images and pages, and it's a lot of work to clean up all that debris. A VM set up this way guarantees your real machine was never touched, and the next boot starts fresh from the master image.
Not ideal if you want to keep your work, though.
True. And VMware knows the world is catching up. Microsoft bought Connectix, which became its Virtual PC line, and is giving a player away free. VMware's player can even run Virtual PC images.
The formats are that close?
VMware reverse-engineered Microsoft's deeply.

beats.title: Snapshots
beats.t: Snapshots save a VM's exact state so you can return to it instantly. Security researchers analyze malware this way: infect a VM, watch it, then roll back to a clean snapshot in seconds.
With the free player, you can't create images. You need someone else's?
Right, but that's where it gets cool. The player is about 30MB, but it installs deeply: virtual network adapters, and a reboot. Not something to try casually.
VMware's site lists maybe 50 or 60 "appliances," ready-made virtual machines from other people, including many flavors of UNIX and Linux. Is it pronounced Ubuntu?
Ubuntu, the Linux I use and love. Mark Shuttleworth, who made a fortune in the dot-com boom, funds it, and it's free. They'll even mail you a disc.
There's a ready-to-go Firefox browser appliance built on Ubuntu, and it works perfectly. It's a 271MB download that unzips to a gigabyte.
And since Ubuntu is free, there's no licensing problem.
It has the GNOME desktop and looks very Windows-like. I installed its calculator through the package manager, which uses Debian .deb files.
It uses apt-get. I put Ubuntu on my old PowerBook, but I could have just used this.
That's what I wanted listeners to know. You don't need a spare machine or a dual boot to play with Linux.
I'd look beyond the default browser appliance, though. It's an older Ubuntu with just Firefox.
I saw one that can install Opera 9. And PC-BSD, a well-reviewed FreeBSD with a full GUI. FreeBSD is my favorite UNIX.
People always ask: can a virus cross from the virtual machine into your real one?
Just don't pull programs out of the VM onto your real machine. Access to your real drives is off by default, though the technology supports drag and drop.
The OS inside has no idea it isn't booting on a real machine. Malware in there thinks it's having a party, but it's a virtual party. VMware intercepts every contact with physical memory and devices.
It also presents the most standard, generic hardware, a standard USB controller and a generic Ethernet card every OS supports, so there are no driver issues.
As long as the player supports your real hardware.
The browser appliance was set to save its state, so when I closed it and ran it again, it continued exactly where I left off.

beats.title: VM escapes
beats.t: Escapes are rare but possible. Flaws in virtual devices have occasionally let code break out to the host. Keep virtualization software updated, and don't share folders with a VM you use for risky browsing.
How much does Workstation cost?
About $199, and it's a godsend for experiments. It's also making a serious dent in corporate computing, running many servers inside one.
There's also Virtual PC and Parallels, which also has Windows and Linux versions. It's getting crowded. Anyone concerned about security should try the free player and browser appliance.
You'll want a gigabyte of disk for it, and plenty of RAM.
I own Parallels, but I'll probably get VMware for the Mac for the cross-platform compatibility.
Parallels is only about $40. But one copy of Windows or Linux that runs on all my machines would be really cool.
Next week: lighter-weight sandboxing that doesn't need a whole VMware or Virtual PC.
And I've been lazy about posting SpinRite testimonials. We get so many that the page is getting too long.
Take off the old ones.
But the old ones are good too.

quiz.q: What's the simplest definition of a virtual machine?
options: Software pretending to be a computer, running inside a real one
quiz.explain: Its value for security is that the software inside can be constrained.

quiz.q: Why is VMware losing some of its early advantage?
options: New Intel and AMD chips support virtualization in hardware
quiz.explain: VMware's workarounds for hostile hardware matter less as chips change.

quiz.q: What does VMware ESX do differently from Workstation?
options: Installs directly on bare hardware with no host OS
quiz.explain: Hosting companies can run up to 128 VMs on one server.

quiz.q: How can a VM help you browse without leaving tracks?
options: Set it to discard all changes, so every session starts from the original image
quiz.explain: Nothing you do touches your real machine.

options: A ready-made virtual machine you can run in the free Player
quiz.explain: Steve tried an Ubuntu-based Firefox browser appliance.

quiz.q: What's the main precaution when surfing inside a VM?
options: Don't copy programs out of the VM onto your real machine
quiz.explain: Malware inside is contained unless you carry it out yourself.
